b: Titled Tuesday (TT) on November 10 came down to tiebreaks between GMs Denis Lazavik and Sina Movahed, two players who also figure to feature prominently in the upcoming Speed Chess Championship (SCC), and it was ultimately Movahed who grabbed first place. The win was his fourth in Titled Tuesday this year, joining GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda at the top of the year's TT wins list.

While the SCC field is already decided, Titled Tuesday continues to contribute to the 2026-27 CCT Standings and 2027 Esports World Cup qualification. Movahed is now in second place behind GM Hikaru Nakamura, with Lazavik in third.
Game And Move Of The Day

For now, Titled Tuesday is responsible for all of each player's CCT points. Later, SCC and Chess.com Open performances will also contribute, although unlike last year's events, top finishers aren't guaranteed a spot beyond what their CCT points get them.

Movahed was one of 16 players to start on 4/4, but Lazavik had already made two draws and was only on 3/4. While it didn't stop him from tying for first, the slightly slower start may have cost him the tiebreaks.

In the fifth round, Movahed lost to GM Christopher Yoo, but a seventh-round draw was the only other blemish on Movahed's record. It was actually another Iranian player, GM Amin Tabatabaei, who became the biggest threat to this week's $6,000 perfect score bounty. He reached 7/7 with impressive wins like his fifth-round victory over GM Karthikeyan Murali, where he gained a solid edge via tactical means on moves 18-21 and converted without issue.

Two rounds after that, Tabatabaei defeated GM Alexey Sarana in round seven. Despite falling behind on the clock early, he made up that time deficit and more, and then won with better endgame play. But that would be the end of his lead, which a third under-30 Iranian star, GM Parham Maghsoodloo, claimed next. Their eighth-round game turned on moves 33-37 before ending on move 40.

Maghsoodloo's next win was even more impressive, taking the black pieces and outplaying Nakamura in an endgame while retaining a clock advantage throughout. By now, only GM Sam Sevian was within half a point, and Maghsoodloo next got White in their matchup.
And here the tide would turn once again. Sevian played slowly but solidly, and, like the tortoise against the hare, his steady approach paid off with a victory.

Sevian now led outright, and was a victory in the last round away from winning the tournament, with White against Lazavik. On the next board, Maghsoodloo tried to recover with Black against countryman Movahed. One of these four players was going to win the tournament.

Sevian almost immediately misstepped, however, with 12.Nf5, following a GM Ben Finegold rule and looking strong, but failing to 12...Qa5. Meanwhile, Movahed was taking a small edge over Maghsoodloo, then a big one once Maghsoodloo self-forked with 18...Nf5 and 19...Rf8. Suddenly, however, Sevian was surviving, but the pressure was still on after Movahed sealed the deal in his game:
Lazavik soon recouped his earlier gains, and the game came down to a time scramble, but Lazavik converted cleanly.

Even if his win delivered first place to Movahed, Lazavik's second place was a strong finish. Sevian's nine points stayed good enough for sixth place and a handful of CCT points. GMs Dmitry Andreikin, Sarana, and Jeffery Xiong finished in the three spots ahead of him, with Nakamura and GM Alexander Grischuk also scoring nine points to take seventh and eighth. Maghsoodloo and GM Dmitrij Kollars also picked up a CCT point to wrap up the top 10. WIM Margarita Potapova won the women's prize.
